summary: load (Fr) (Class I lever) is what the Fulcrum calculator works out, and it gets there from the effort (Fₑ) and the length of the lever (L). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Fulcrum calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fulcrum calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports load (Fr) (Class I lever) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the lever class); then you type in the effort (Fₑ) (Class I lever), the length of the lever (L) (Class I lever), the mechanical advantage (Class I lever) and the load (Fr) (Class II lever).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fulcrum calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Load (Fr)=effort (Fₑ) × mechanical advantage
Length of the load arm (dr)=length of the lever (L) ÷ (mechanical advantage + 1)
Length of the effort arm (dₑ)=length of the lever (L) − length of the load arm (dr)
Length of the load arm (dr)=length of the lever (L) ÷ mechanical advantage
Length of the effort arm (dₑ)=length of the lever (L)
Length of the lever (L)=length of the load arm (dr)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Lever class set to Class I: Effort - Fulcrum - Load, Effort (Fₑ) = 10 N and Mechanical advantage = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Load (Fr) = 100 N.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Load (Fr) = 100 N should be roughly the size you expected from Lever class set to Class I: Effort - Fulcrum - Load and Effort (Fₑ) = 10 N.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fulcrum calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the effort (Fₑ) and the length of the lever (L) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fulcrum calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns load (Fr) (Class I lever), derived from the effort (Fₑ) and the length of the lever (L). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fulcrum calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the effort (Fₑ) and the length of the lever (L), which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter load (Fr) (Class I lever) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Load (Fr) (Class I lever) opens in newtons and the chip beside it offers 16 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Load (Fr) = 100 N. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fulcrum calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
